s0001: Choosing the correct method for subtracting fractions with different denominators (finding a common denominator)
s0002: Rewrite the fractions with a common denominator: multiply the numerator and denominator of each fraction by the denominator of the other fraction, then subtract the new numerators.
s0003: What is the correct way to find the difference $\frac{2}{5} - \frac{1}{3}$?
s0004: The denominators five and three are different, so we take their product, fifteen, as the common denominator.
s0005: We multiply the numerator and denominator of the first fraction by three, and those of the second by five; the values of the fractions do not change.
s0006: Now the denominators are the same, so we subtract the numerators and get one fifteenth.
s0008: So the correct method is option C.
s0009: A student who chose A subtracted the numerators and the denominators separately; fractions cannot be subtracted that way.
s0010: A student who chose B multiplied the denominators correctly, but subtracted the numerators without adjusting them to the new denominator.
s0011: A student who chose D multiplied each numerator by the denominator of its own fraction; each numerator should be multiplied by the denominator of the other fraction.
s0012: First change both fractions into fractions with the same denominator; only then can you subtract.
s0013: What is the correct way to calculate the difference $\frac{3}{4} - \frac{2}{7}$?
s0014: The denominators are four and seven, so the common denominator is twenty-eight.
s0015: We multiply the first fraction by seven over seven, and the second by four over four.
s0016: We subtract the numerators: twenty-one minus eight is thirteen, so the result is thirteen twenty-eighths.
s0018: The correct method is option A.
s0019: A student who chose B found the common denominator but forgot to multiply the numerators.
s0020: A student who chose C multiplied each numerator by its own denominator, and as a result the numerator even comes out negative.
s0021: A student who chose D subtracted the numerators and the denominators separately.
s0022: Remember that when you rewrite a fraction, the numerator and the denominator are multiplied by the same number.
s0023: Using fractions and percentages of a number and the properties of multiplication to identify a true number sentence
s0024: Calculate the left side and the right side of each equation separately (changing each percentage into hundredths), and check in which equation the two sides are equal.
s0025: Which of these number sentences is true?
s0029: In option A, the left side is twenty-four and the right side is eight tenths, so they are not equal.
s0030: In option B, both sides equal twenty-four: in fact, it is just four times six and six times four.
s0031: In option C, we get one point two and four point eight, so they are not equal.
s0032: In option D, division is not commutative, so the results are different.
s0034: So the true number sentence is option B.
s0035: A student who chose A saw that the fraction $\frac{2}{5}$ equals $40\%$, but did not pay attention to which number the part is taken of.
s0036: A student who chose C thought that because both numbers were doubled, the result would not change; in fact, the result becomes four times as large.
s0037: A student who chose D thought that, as in multiplication, the numbers in a division can be swapped.
s0038: Calculate each side separately and compare the results.
s0042: In option A, we get twenty-eight and two point eight, so they are not equal.
s0043: In option B, swapping the numbers in a subtraction changes the result.
s0044: In option C, both sides equal fifteen: each is seventy-five times twenty divided by one hundred.
s0045: In option D, we get two and eight, so they are not equal.
s0047: The true number sentence is option C.
s0048: A student who chose A replaced $\frac{7}{10}$ with $40\%$ instead of $70\%$ and was misled by the swapped digits.
s0049: A student who chose B thought that subtraction, like addition, is commutative.
s0050: A student who chose D saw that both the number and the percentage were doubled and concluded that the result would not change; in fact, it becomes four times as large.
s0051: Remember that a percent of a number is that many hundredths of it, and calculate both sides.
s0052: Writing the area of a figure as an algebraic expression: subtracting the area of a path from the area of a rectangle and simplifying
s0053: Write the area of the whole rectangle (length × width), subtract the area of the path (length × width), and combine like terms.
s0054:
The picture shows a rectangular garden plot. Its length is $(x + 6)$ m and its width is $x$ m. The white path that crosses the plot is also rectangular, and it is 2 m wide.
Which expression gives the area of the green part of the plot (in m²)?
s0057: The area of the whole plot is its length times its width: x squared plus six x.
s0059: The path runs across the whole width of the plot: it is x meters long and two meters wide, so its area is two x.
s0060: We subtract the area of the path from the whole area: six x minus two x is four x.
s0062: The area of the green part is x squared plus four x, which is option C.
s0063: A student who chose A found the area of the whole plot but forgot to subtract the area of the path.
s0064: A student who chose B took the area of the path to be 2, not taking into account that the path is x long.
s0065: A student who chose D subtracted the area of the path correctly, but then also subtracted another 2.
s0066: The path is also a rectangle: one side is 2 m. What is the other side equal to?
s0067:
The picture shows a rectangular flower bed. Its width is $x$ m and its length is $(x + 3)$ m. A white path 1 m wide crosses the flower bed along its width.
Which expression gives the area of the green part of the flower bed (in m²)?
s0069: The area of the whole flower bed: we multiply the width x by the length x plus three.
s0071: The length of the path equals the width of the flower bed, x meters, and it is one meter wide, so its area is x.
s0072: We subtract the area of the path from the whole area: three x minus x is two x.
s0074: The area of the green part is x squared plus two x, which is option B.
s0075: A student who chose A took the area of the path to be 1 m², forgetting that it is x long.
s0076: A student who chose C found the area of the whole flower bed and did not subtract the area of the path.
s0077: A student who chose D added the area of the path instead of subtracting it.
s0078: Green part = whole rectangle minus path; you can find the length of the path from the picture.

s0101: Writing and solving an equation when the lengths of the pieces are given as algebraic expressions, and finding the longest piece
s0102: Set the sum of the lengths of all the pieces equal to the total length, solve the equation to find x, then work out the length of each piece and choose the largest.
s0103:
Malika cut a 60 cm atlas silk ribbon into 3 pieces.
The lengths of the pieces (in cm) are $2x - 10$, $x + 6$ and $x + 4$.
How many centimeters long is the longest piece?
s0105: Together, the three pieces make up the whole ribbon, so we set their sum equal to sixty.
s0106: We combine like terms: the x terms give four x, and the numbers minus ten, six and four add up to zero.
s0107: Dividing sixty by four, we find that x equals fifteen.
s0108: We work out each piece: twenty, twenty-one and nineteen; check: the total is sixty.
s0110: The longest piece is twenty-one centimeters.
s0111: Many students write x = 15 as the answer, or think the expression with 2x is the longest and answer 20 cm; you need to work out each piece and compare.
s0112: After finding x, work out the lengths of all three pieces.
s0113:
Jasur divided a 72 m wire into 3 pieces.
The lengths of the pieces (in m) are $2x - 12$, $x + 9$ and $x + 7$.
How many meters long is the longest piece?
s0114: The sum of the lengths of the pieces equals the whole wire, that is, seventy-two.
s0115: We combine like terms: four x plus four.
s0116: We subtract four from both sides and divide sixty-eight by four: x is seventeen.
s0117: The pieces are twenty-two, twenty-six and twenty-four meters; the total is seventy-two.
s0119: The longest piece is twenty-six meters.
s0120: Typical mistakes: writing x = 17 as the answer, or assuming the piece with 2x is the longest and answering 22 m.
s0121: To write the equation, add all the pieces and set the sum equal to the total length.
s0122: Using the fact that the height of an isosceles triangle equals half of its base to find an angle with logical reasoning
s0123: The height divides the base of an isosceles triangle into two equal parts; if half of the base equals the height, the right triangles formed are isosceles, and each of their acute angles is 45°.
s0124:
In triangle KLM in the picture:
KM = LM,
MH is the height drawn to side KL,
side KL is 2 times as long as MH.
What is the measure of angle KML in degrees?
s0125: In an isosceles triangle, the height drawn to the base divides the base into two equal parts.
s0126: The base is twice as long as the height, so its half, KH, equals the height MH.
s0127: KHM is an isosceles right triangle, so each of its acute angles is forty-five degrees.
s0128: In the same way, in triangle LHM the angle at M is forty-five degrees.
s0129: We add the two angles and get ninety degrees.
s0132: Many students answer 45° (only half of the angle), or think the triangle is equilateral and answer 60°.

s0142: We subtract ninety from one hundred eighty and divide by two: forty-five degrees.
s0144: The angle at vertex D is forty-five degrees.

s0172: Finding the side of a square from its perimeter, and then its area
s0173: Divide the perimeter by 4 to find the side of the square, then multiply the side by itself to find the area.
s0174:
The perimeter of a square is 28 cm.
What is the area of this square?
s0180: A square has four equal sides, so we divide the perimeter by four to find the side: seven centimeters.
s0182: The area equals the side squared: seven times seven is forty-nine.
s0184: The area of the square is forty-nine square centimeters, which is option C.

s0186: A student who chose B divided the perimeter by 2 instead of 4 to find the side, and then squared 14.

s0193: The area of the plot is one hundred twenty-one square meters, which is option D.

s0198: Finding the greatest number of identical objects that fit in a box shaped like a rectangular prism by matching their dimensions
s0199: Check which dimension of the box each dimension of the object fits into exactly (with no remainder) and choose the best arrangement; multiply the numbers in each direction and check using the ratio of the volumes.
s0200:
Aziz is packing books of the same size into a box shaped like a rectangular prism.
The dimensions of each book are 20 cm, 16 cm and 5 cm. The inside dimensions of the box are 48 cm, 30 cm and 20 cm.
What is the greatest number of books that can fit in the box?
s0209: We place the books so that each dimension fits into a dimension of the box with no remainder: twenty goes with twenty, sixteen with forty-eight, and five with thirty.
s0210: That fits one, three and six books in the three directions.
s0212: Let's check: the volume of the box is exactly eighteen times the volume of a book, so no space is left over and no more books can fit.
s0214: The greatest number of books that can fit in the box is eighteen.
s0215: Many students place the books as shown in the picture ($48 : 20 = 2$, $20 : 5 = 4$, $30 : 16 = 1$) and answer only 8; they do not consider that the books can be turned.
s0216: Turn the book and check which dimension of the box each of its dimensions divides into with no remainder.
s0217:
Small boxes of tea, all the same size, were delivered to a teahouse in a crate.
The dimensions of each tea box are 12 cm, 8 cm and 5 cm. The inside dimensions of the crate are 36 cm, 25 cm and 24 cm.
What is the greatest number of tea boxes that can be packed into the crate?
s0225: We match each dimension with one it divides into evenly: twelve with thirty-six, five with twenty-five, and eight with twenty-four.
s0226: That fits three, five and three tea boxes in the three directions.
s0228: The ratio of the volumes is also forty-five, so the crate is completely full and no more can fit.
s0229: The greatest number of tea boxes that fit in the crate is forty-five.
s0230: Typical mistake: placing the tea boxes as shown in the picture ($36 : 12 = 3$, $24 : 5 = 4$, $25 : 8 = 3$) and getting 36.

s0232: Understanding that in an experiment with replacement the probability of the next event does not depend on the previous result, and calculating the probability
s0233: Because the item taken out is put back, the contents of the container do not change; probability = number of favorable outcomes : number of all possible outcomes.
s0234:
A box contains 12 pens: 4 are green and 8 are black.
Malika took one pen from the box at random. It was green. Malika put the pen back in the box.
What is the probability that the next pen she takes at random will be green?
s0235: The box again has 12 pens: 4 green, 8 black
s0236: The pen was put back, so the pens in the box did not change.
s0237: There are four green pens and twelve pens in total.
s0238: We simplify the fraction by dividing by four: one third.
s0240: The probability is one third, which is option B.
s0241: A student who chose A assumed the pen was not put back: 3 green pens and 11 in total.
s0242: A student who chose C found the probability of taking one particular pen and ignored the number of green pens.
s0243: A student who chose D divided the number of green pens by the number of black pens instead of the total.
s0244: Think about how many green pens and how many pens in total are in the box after the pen is put back.

s0247: The checker was put back, so the contents of the bag did not change.
s0248: There are six white checkers and ten in total.
s0249: Simplifying by dividing by two gives three fifths.

s0256: Analyzing a population age structure chart to explain why the population grows faster in a country with a larger share of young people
s0257: Compare the shares of the age groups in the two countries: the population grows faster where the share of young people (0–19) who will have children in the future is larger. The chart shows percentages, not total numbers.

Why is the population of country P expected to grow faster than that of country Q?
s0259: Age structure of the populations of countries P and Q
s0266: The total population of country P is larger than that of Q.
s0267: In country P, the share of people aged 0–19 (48%) is much larger than in Q (20%), so there are relatively more young people who will start families and have children in the coming years.
s0268: Because the share of older people in country Q is large, more children will be born there.
s0269: The share of people aged 20–59 in country P is larger than in Q.
s0271: We read the first group from the chart: forty-eight percent in P, but only twenty percent in Q.
s0272: The share of older people is the other way around: it is much larger in Q.
s0273: Many young people $\Rightarrow$ many families and children in the future
s0274: Today's children and teenagers will start families in a few years, so more children will be born in the country with a larger share of young people.

The fractions $\frac{9}{12}$ and $\frac{\square}{28}$ are equal.
What is the value of $\square$?
s0368: We simplify nine twelfths by dividing by three: three fourths.
s0369: To make the denominator twenty-eight, we multiply it by seven.
s0370: We multiply the numerator by seven too: twenty-one.
s0372: The square stands for twenty-one, which is option D.
s0373: A student who chose A gave the difference of the denominators ($28 - 12 = 16$) as the answer.
s0374: A student who chose B added 16 to the numerator because 16 was added to the denominator: $9 + 16 = 25$.
s0375: A student who chose C found the multiplier and wrote it as the answer without multiplying the numerator.
s0376: In equivalent fractions, the numerator and denominator are multiplied or divided by the same number, not added to.
